pr_title: service: do fine-grained validation of CPUSchedulingPriority= at execution time
pr_body:
The precise bounds of the scheduling priority depend on the scheduling policy, so depending on the order in which the two settings are specified the validation might pass or fail.
When checking the setting only validate the outer range (valid values in general are 0 to 99), and let the execution fail later if the priority does not match the specified policy (1 to 99 for RR/FIFO, 0 for the rest).

Fixes https://github.com/systemd/systemd/issues/20320
pr_comments: Not exactly familiar with this stuff, so this might be a stupid question, but what do you mean by fail later? Do we have another check in systemd later or do you mean the kernel will return an error later when we try to apply these values and they're out of the valid range?

> Not exactly familiar with this stuff, so this might be a stupid question, but what do you mean by fail later? Do we have another check in systemd later or do you mean the kernel will return an error later when we try to apply these values and they're out of the valid range?

The latter - it's nice to provide an error on configuration when possible, but in this case it depends on other settings and the order is not fixed, so we'll let it fail when the service is started and the final configuration is applied

hmm, i think either we should output a clear error message if we detect invalid policies configured and we can't set them, or better: handle the issue gracefully and set the priority 0 if the priority is not defined for one of the policies... (and maybe warn)

right now they'll just see EINVAL if things fail, right, which isn't much better than the status quo ante?

> hmm, i think either we should output a clear error message if we detect invalid policies configured and we can't set them, or better: handle the issue gracefully and set the priority 0 if the priority is not defined for one of the policies... (and maybe warn)
> 
> right now they'll just see EINVAL if things fail, right, which isn't much better than the status quo ante?

Well no, the status quo before was that depending on the order in which you list the policy and priority settings (in the unit or command line for sd-run) things might or might not work.
With this change, correct configuration now will always work regardless of ordering.

The case where you had the wrong configuration values, but in the right order, got slightly worse as it will now error out on service start, rather than being refused at config time.

issue_context.title: Unable to set systemd service with realtime scheduler and priority
issue_context.body:
> `systemd 247 (247.2-5~bpo10+1)`

<!-- **NOTE:** Do not submit bug reports about anything but the two most recently released *major* systemd versions upstream! -->
<!--           If there have been multiple stable releases for that major version, please consider updating to a recent one before reporting an issue. -->
<!--           When using a distro package, please make sure that the version reported is meaningful for upstream. -->
<!-- See https://github.com/systemd/systemd-stable/releases for the list of most recent releases. -->
<!-- For older version please use distribution trackers (see https://systemd.io/CONTRIBUTING#filing-issues). -->

**Used distribution**
 > `debian`

**Linux kernel version used** (`uname -a`)
<!-- Make sure to enclose the pasted kernel version in `backticks`, so that
     GitHub doesn't convert the `#` character typically included in it into a
     reference to old GitHub issues. -->
 > `Linux controller 5.4.91-bone-rt-r43 #1buster PREEMPT_RT Sat Jan 30 03:27:21 UTC 2021 armv7l GNU/Linux`

**CPU architecture issue was seen on**
 > `ARMv7 Processor rev 2 (v7l)`
(also able to reproduce on)
 > `Intel(R) Core(TM) i7-3820 CPU @ 3.60GHz`

**Expected behaviour you didn't see**

The description below is a minimal reproduction of a larger problem of being unable to set real-time scheduling on a systemd service file. I unfortunately do not have access to a test environment and therefore found the latest version of systemd I could find (which doesn't quite meet the 2 major revision requirement), but as far as I can tell, no issues matching `CPUSchedulingPolicy` have been filed or fixed since.

**Steps to reproduce the problem**
Please find below the minimal reproducible bug, as well as what I believe is causing the bug.

Running as root:
 > `$ systemd-run --pty --quiet --property=CPUSchedulingPolicy=rr  --property=RestrictRealtime=false --property=LimitRTPRIO=infinity /usr/bin/chrt -p 0`

correctly yields

> pid 27173's current scheduling policy: SCHED_RR
> pid 27173's current scheduling priority: 1

> `$ systemd-run --pty --quiet --property=CPUSchedulingPolicy=rr  --property=RestrictRealtime=false --property=LimitRTPRIO=infinity /usr/bin/chrt --rr 80 /usr/bin/chrt -p 0`

correctly yields

> pid 13806's current scheduling policy: SCHED_RR
> pid 13806's current scheduling priority: 80

However:
> `$ systemd-run --pty --quiet --property=CPUSchedulingPolicy=rr --property=CPUSchedulingPriority=80 --property=RestrictRealtime=false --property=LimitRTPRIO=infinity /usr/bin/chrt -p 0`

incorrectly yeilds:
> `Failed to start transient service unit: Invalid CPU scheduling priority: 80`


I believe I have isolated the bug itself [here](https://github.com/systemd/systemd/blob/80362ec56fc993d1464ae438fcfcb6f763bff1ac/src/core/dbus-execute.c#L2617).

**Additional program output to the terminal or log subsystem illustrating the issue**

Using the following short program
```C++
#include <stdio.h>
#include <sched.h>
int main(int argc, char* argv[])
{
        int scheduler = sched_getscheduler(0);
        printf("%d %d %d\n", scheduler, sched_get_priority_min(scheduler), sched_get_priority_max(scheduler));
}
```

Running as root, interactive user, I get:
> `$ ./a.out`
> `0 0 0`

(which corresponds to the "OTHER" scheduler)

> `systemd-run --pty --quiet --property=CPUSchedulingPolicy=rr --property=RestrictRealtime=false --property=LimitRTPRIO=infinity ./a.out`

correctly yields:
> `2 1 99`

and furthermore `strace`'ing the `systemd` process shows:
> `sched_get_priority_min(SCHED_RR)      = 1`
> `sched_get_priority_max(SCHED_RR)      = 99`


But when `CPUSchedulingPriority` is specified as previously mentioned, systemd fails to launch the process and I can see through `strace` that both [`sched_get_priority_min`](https://github.com/systemd/systemd/blob/80362ec56fc993d1464ae438fcfcb6f763bff1ac/src/core/dbus-execute.c#L2614) and `sched_get_priority_max` are called with `SCHED_OTHER` (0) as inputs and both result in `0` (as per interactive call to ./a.out).

This makes sense given code on line 2616 is `p < min || p > max` is always true if `min == max`.

I believe what's happening is that the SchedulingPriority is being set before the Policy.


----------

Also, for what it's worth, this is related to issue #10290 and the code introduced to fix it: https://github.com/systemd/systemd/pull/10292/commits/2926f407828988e9fbef2b3614f5ba8569f1bbfd
comments: Yeah, this is broken. The validation of the range needs to take place after all props are passed.

review_comments: these boundaries really should be macros, that come with an explanation that they are the min/max for all known policies.
